name: Deliberative democracy
summary: Deliberative democracy holds that democratic decisions gain legitimacy from public reasoning among free and equal citizens who give each other reasons, and not from the aggregation of votes or bargaining among interests. Its ideal procedure gives all participants equal standing and voice, protects expression regardless of content, and requires that wealth not shape who can take part, which Cohen says may call for public funding of parties and limits on private political spending. It is institutionally flexible: where consensus fails it falls back on majority rule, and its advocates propose parties, civil society and randomly selected citizens' assemblies.
scope: The liberal-egalitarian deliberative tradition as the defining sources present it: Joshua Cohen's 1989 account of the ideal deliberative procedure, Habermas's discourse theory of democracy (SEP), Gutmann and Thompson's reciprocity, publicity and accountability, and Fishkin's deliberative assemblies (as reported by openDemocracy). It excludes agonistic critics such as Mouffe, and other thinkers' wider theories (Rawls's two principles of justice are not the ideology's, only what Cohen draws from them). The theory is chiefly about how decisions are made, so most policy statements are null.

missingStatements.text: Laws should be justified by reasons that all citizens, as free and equals, could reasonably accept.
missingStatements.rationale: Cohen's legitimacy principle and Habermas's democratic principle both make justification to all citizens the test of legitimate law.

missingStatements.text: Randomly selected groups of citizens should be used to deliberate on, and help decide, major policy questions.
missingStatements.rationale: Deliberative polling, citizens' assemblies and sortition-based bodies are the central practical proposals of the Fishkin and Landemore wing.

missingStatements.text: Wealth should be prevented from giving some citizens much more political influence than others.
missingStatements.rationale: Cohen requires substantive equality in which the distribution of resources does not shape deliberative opportunity, and endorses limits on private political spending and public party funding.

notes: Themes searched in the saved sources (Cohen 1989, SEP Democracy, SEP Habermas, Hauptli on Gutmann and Thompson, Weir on Fishkin): government and procedure, liberty and expression, equality and franchise, economy and wealth, religion, world, society. Most statements outside procedure, equality and expression are null because the defining sources record no position. Internal differences (Fishkin and Cohen on mass participation versus assemblies, Habermas's two-track model, agonist critics) are not scored as splits where the sources do not take opposite positions on a statement. Later pass: 178 earlier answers were nulled (inferences from Rawls or Habermas as individuals, zeros without evidence on both sides, Wikipedia-only answers) and the earlier slideshare copy of Bohman (s4) is no longer relied on; it and the Rawls entry (s6) remain listed only as sources of the replaced versions in the talk pages. Not-found: no open-access English full text of Cohen 1989 was fetched (Spanish translation used).
